findings.title: Omitted signal–noise terms falsify the main oracle bound
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-bigot11a__I01 — Omitted signal–noise terms falsify the main oracle bound
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem8 and Equation(18), PDF page10 / journal p.3196, Section3.2; the model decomposition in Equation(4), PDF page4 / p.3190, and Equation(8), page5 / p.3191; AppendixA.5, Equation(42), PDF page32 / p.3218.

**Claim.** Under the additive observation model, Assumptions1–2 and positive-definite Gaussian noise covariance, Theorem8 gives a sparse oracle bound for
\(n^{-1}\|\widehat\Sigma_\lambda-\Sigma\|_F^2\)
with probability at least \(1-M^{1-\delta}\). Its right side combines sparse approximation error, \(\|S-\Sigma\|_F^2/n\), and a term proportional to \(\|\Sigma_{\rm noise}\|_2^2s/n\), with its prescribed penalty and stated constants.

**Error and evidence.** For the stated observations \(\widetilde X_i=X_i+E_i\), the correct identity is

\[
\widetilde S=S+W+V,\qquad
V=\frac1N\sum_i(X_iE_i^\top+E_iX_i^\top).
\]

Equations(4),(8),(42) omit \(V\). Independence makes its expectation zero, and does not remove the realized fluctuation. The following finite counterexample disproves the stated bound itself.

Take \(n=M=4,N=2,G=I_4,s=1,\epsilon=1,\delta=3\). Let \(r_i\) be independent fair Rademacher signs and set

\[
X_i=1000r_ie_1,\qquad E_i\overset{\rm iid}{\sim}N(0,I_4),
\]

with all signs and noise independent. A finite design \(T=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and coordinate dictionary realize this process. It is mean zero and bounded, so Assumption2 holds: for example \(\rho(\Sigma)=1001\) and \(\alpha=2\) suffice. Assumption1 holds with \(\theta(G)=0\), \(\rho_{\min}(s)=\rho_{\max}(G^\top G)=G_{\max}=1\), \(c_0=7\) and \(\kappa_{s,c_0}^2=1\). The noise covariance is positive definite. Only the noise covariance is required to be positive definite; the rank-one signal is expressly admissible.

Here

\[
S=\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(10^6,0,0,0)
\]

for every realized signal sample. The comparator \(\Psi=\Sigma\) has sparsity1 and zero approximation error. Both of the first two oracle terms therefore vanish. The prescribed quantities are

\[
\gamma_k=2,\quad
\lambda=(1+\sqrt2+\sqrt{3\log4})^2<25,\quad C(1)=144.
\]

Evaluating the infimum at this comparator bounds the asserted right side by

\[
\frac{(1+1)144\lambda^2}{4}=72\lambda^2<45000.
\]

Now use the **genuine minimizer over symmetric matrices** in Equation(7). Its strongly convex quadratic loss guarantees a unique minimizer. Varying its diagonal coordinate, and using the unit-norm bound on a column-norm subgradient, yields

\[
|\widehat\Psi_{11}-\widetilde S_{11}|\le2\lambda.
\]

This is a valid KKT consequence on the symmetric domain and does not use Proposition1. Define

\[
z=(r_1E_{11}+r_2E_{21})/2\sim N(0,1/2).
\]

Then

\[
\widetilde S_{11}-10^6=2000z+(E_{11}^2+E_{21}^2)/2.
\]

On \(z\ge1/4\), the nonnegative last term and the KKT bound imply

\[
\widehat\Psi_{11}-10^6\ge500-2\lambda>450,
\qquad
\frac14\|\widehat\Psi-\Sigma\|_F^2>50625>45000.
\]

The Gaussian density of \(z\) is bounded by \(1/\sqrt\pi\), giving

\[
P(z\ge1/4)\ge\frac12-\frac1{4\sqrt\pi}>0.35.
\]

Theorem8 permits failure probability only \(4^{1-3}=1/16\). Thus it fails substantially more often than claimed. This is an analytic counterexample, rather than a rare numerical optimizer failure. Arithmetic checks give \(\lambda=19.83409\), asserted comparator bound28324.15, error lower bound52976.35 on the event, and event probability0.36184.

**Reason for rejection.** The central theoretical contribution is a noisy covariance oracle guarantee supporting the subsequent support-selection and operator-norm analysis. The guarantee is false under its own assumptions. More generally, increase the bounded signal amplitude while retaining this construction: \(S-\Sigma\) and the approximation term stay zero, while the omitted fluctuation grows and the prescribed penalty/right side remain noise-only. Changing a fixed constant cannot restore that statement. Repair requires controlling the missing cross terms and changing the claimed variance/penalty dependence or admissible model. That is a substantive replacement of the main noisy-data guarantee and warrants rejection as written. No assertion is made that every historical empirical result fails or that the fixed-support projection identity is invalid.

**Discovery method.** Expanded the additive observations while tracing the matrix-regression decomposition, then traced the missing terms to the proof’s noise-only event.

**Verification method.** Read all39 journal pages and AppendixA; rechecked the original rendered model, theorem and proof. Derived the finite counterexample and symmetric-coordinate KKT bound; ran the saved analytic/arithmetic controls. An independent reviewer checked the original assumptions and repeated the derivation. An author-hosted final preprint and arXivv2 retain the same missing-term identity. No unavailable historical MATLAB execution is used as evidence.

**Reproduction artifacts.** `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`, `exact-controls.json`, `gentile-independent-qa.md`, `gentile-independent-qa.py`, and `gentile-independent-results.json`. Execute the control with Python plus NumPy/SciPy; the displayed analytic inequalities require no solver.

**Confidence: High.** Exact admissible construction, strict inequality margins, and an analytic probability contradiction independently verified against the original PDF. The proof applies to the defined symmetric estimator, independently of the paper’s separate closed-form symmetry defect.

findings.title: Supervised discretization uses evaluation labels in the headline benchmark
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-carvalho11a__I01 — Supervised discretization uses evaluation labels in the headline benchmark
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 5, PDF page 16 / printed page 2196, including footnote 5, specifies supervised entropy-based discretization using `weka.filters.supervised.attribute.Discretize`. PDF page 18 / printed page 2198 specifies the subsequent holdout and five-fold cross-validation comparisons and paired significance tests. The affected results are Figures 4–5 (PDF pages 19–20), Tables 3–4 (PDF page 21), and the comparative conclusions on PDF pages 19 and 22. Their prominence is explicit in the abstract (PDF page 1), introduction (PDF page 3), and conclusion (PDF page 22).

**Affected claim.** The new surrogate's predictive merits are supported by a 25-dataset comparison claiming statistically significant superiority over generatively trained Bayesian networks, C4.5, nearest-neighbor and logistic-regression classifiers, and accuracy comparable with expensive discriminative estimators/SVMs. These are inductive prediction comparisons: training is followed by prediction on held-out cases or held-out folds. Supervised preprocessing must therefore be fitted using each training partition's labels, then applied to its evaluation partition.

**Demonstrated error and primary attribution.** The released preprocessing is fitted before these evaluation partitions are withheld. The original text by itself does not explicitly say “fit on every label before splitting.” The authors' primary supplementary release resolves that ambiguity: its *Datasets* section calls the downloadable raw and discretized files the data used in the experiments, and supplies one supervised-discretized ARFF file per full dataset. Its *Running* section then applies the classifier's cross-validation option to the supplied dataset. This page is preserved as `author-fCLL.html` and remains available at [the author's supplementary page](https://www.lx.it.pt/~asmc/software/fCLL.html).

The following independent native checks authenticate the global fit, rather than inferring it from missing driver code:

| Released dataset | Full pool | Training file | Test file | Archived feature-bin codes differing from a native supervised fit on the **full** pool |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| letter | 20,000 | 15,000 | 5,000 | 0 |
| satimage | 6,435 | 4,435 | 2,000 | 0 |
| waveform-21 | 5,000 | 300 | 4,700 | 0 |

For each of these three datasets, the released `.all` raw file is exactly the concatenation of the `.data` and `.test` files. Each attribute is numeric before discretization. Running the untouched released `Discretize` class with its default supervised method on all observations reproduces **every archived feature-bin code**, across every observation and feature. Fitting it only on the training prefix instead changes 3 letter features, 36 satimage features, and 19 waveform features (complete cut-point logs are retained). Thus the archived representation uses the held-out response labels to select cut points. On waveform, 4,700 of the 5,000 labels used to construct this representation belong to the released test partition.

This information survives the classifier's later training split. In the untouched release, `weka.classifiers.Evaluation.crossValidateModel`, lines 510–517, splits the already loaded `Instances` and builds classifiers on those fold subsets. `weka.classifiers.bayes.BayesNet.normalizeDataSet`, lines 231–260, only fits `Discretize` if nonnominal attributes remain. The supplied discretized ARFF attributes are already nominal, so that branch does not refit or undo the full-data cut points. The source code and compiled class files are both preserved in the authentic `WEKA-fCLL.zip` release. This is leakage through a supervised transformation, not harmless use of unlabeled feature locations.

**Reproducible material consequence.** I ran controlled comparisons with the original released compiled WEKA classes, preserving the scoring code, TAN learner, estimator and classifier settings. The only changed operation is whether the supervised discretizer sees the full pool or the training partition. Held-out observations are identical in both arms. On CV datasets the fresh controls use one fixed stratified five-fold split with seed 1. On holdout datasets they use the membership in the recovered raw training/test files. All 25 controls, including cases with no deterioration or changes favoring the new score, are retained in `native-results-v2.json`.

Two of the independently authenticated full-pool datasets give:

| Dataset and native implementation | Full-pool supervised preprocessing | Training-only supervised preprocessing |
|---|---:|---:|
| letter: TAN–fCLL | 4,318 / 5,000 = 86.36% | 4,255 / 5,000 = 85.10% |
| letter: TAN–LL | 4,298 / 5,000 = 85.96% | 4,282 / 5,000 = 85.64% |
| waveform: TAN–fCLL | 3,647 / 4,700 = 77.596% | 3,604 / 4,700 = 76.681% |
| waveform: TAN–LL | 3,527 / 4,700 = 75.043% | 3,702 / 4,700 = 78.766% |

The shared preprocessing affects the algorithms unequally and reverses these relative comparisons. It cannot be justified by saying every classifier receives the same leaked representation. These controlled numbers are **fresh native checks**, not a claim to reproduce every historical split, parameter choice or table entry exactly. In particular, they do not establish the full corrected historical ranking, nor that fCLL is generally inferior. The primary error is the use of evaluation labels; the controls show that its consequences are material for precisely the relative prediction comparison being claimed.

The authentic source also uses a discriminative weight differing slightly from the analytical constant. That local discrepancy is screened separately. A controlled check replacing only those constants by their exact analytical values preserves both reversals: letter counts are unchanged; waveform becomes 3,626/4,700 for training-only TAN–fCLL, still below TAN–LL at 3,702/4,700. It is retained in `exact-weight-results.json` and is not needed to authenticate the preprocessing error.

**Why this warrants rejection as written.** Prediction quality is a coequal headline contribution of this paper. The new score is deliberately heuristic as an approximation to conditional log-likelihood; its correct decomposability, parameter maximization and score-equivalence results do not themselves imply the advertised predictive advantage. That advantage is established through the affected benchmark. Twenty of the 25 released raw datasets contain numeric features subject to supervised discretization, including the large holdout examples above. The combined accuracy plots and significance comparisons therefore do not provide the claimed held-out evidence for inductive classifier superiority or comparability.

Correcting this requires rerunning the supervised preprocessing within every outer training split, and within relevant inner tuning splits, followed by new predictions and comparative significance calculations. The existing reported results cannot be restored by changing a coefficient, caption, p-value convention or local proof step. The fresh ordering reversals demonstrate why the aggregate conclusion cannot simply be carried over. The finding does not assert that the unaffected categorical cases, the mathematical properties of the score, or its computational complexity are false.

**Discovery method.** Read all 30 original pages and both appendices, traced the preprocessing/evaluation order, recovered the author's original supplementary page, software and raw/discretized datasets, and noticed that one supervised representation was supplied for the complete data pool.

**Verification method.** Inspected original rendered PDF pages 14–16 and 18–21; independently regenerated all archived bin codes on the three exact train-plus-test pools with the authentic compiled supervised filter; traced the released cross-validation and nominal-data normalization branches; ran paired native controls with only preprocessing placement changed. Independent 50-digit integration and separate finite probability-table checks preserve the unaffected mathematical score claims. A second reviewer independently inspected the original protocol/claim pages, primary supplement and code paths, and reran the waveform full-pool bin regeneration and paired native evaluation with zero exit status; the results matched. This was targeted verification, not a second full-paper review. See `root-independent-qa.md` and `root-independent-native-check.json`. Scripts, complete logs, downloaded hashes and initial compatibility/alignment failures are saved.

**Confidence: high.** The attribution rests on explicit primary-release descriptions, exact full-pool bin reproduction, and executable native behavior. Historical-fold uncertainty is explicit and is not used as a premise of the leakage finding.

**Evidence and reproduction.** All artifacts are in `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`:

- `author-fCLL.html`, `source-downloads.json`, `WEKA-fCLL.zip`, `original-data.rar`, `discretized-data.rar`, and the extracted unchanged release/data.
- `GlobalCutCheck.java`, `global-cut-check-results.json`, `letter-cut-check.log`, `satimage-cut-check.log`, `waveform-21-cut-check.log`, `holdout-file-check.json`.
- `prepare-raw.py`, `raw-preparation.json`, `AuditCV2.java`, `native-controls-v2.py`, `native-results-v2.json`, `native-logs-v2/`, and `preprocessing-evidence.json`.
- `check.py`, `results.json` for the unaffected analytic and score-equivalence checks; `exact-weight-results.json` for the weight-only control.

To reproduce the native checks, compile `AuditCV2.java` and `GlobalCutCheck.java` against the released `WEKA/bin` directory, run `prepare-raw.py`, then `native-controls-v2.py`. The local harness uses the available Java runtime and ECJ compiler under `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`; only the independent harness requires compilation. It loads the authentic released optimizer/classifier bytecode unchanged. Initial Java-language-level/API compatibility retries and raw/archive row-alignment failures are preserved and excluded from the final controlled results.

Direct reproduction links: bin-regeneration results [unpublished artifact reference omitted], paired native results [unpublished artifact reference omitted], preprocessing summary [unpublished artifact reference omitted], independent verification [unpublished artifact reference omitted], whole-paper checks [unpublished artifact reference omitted].

findings.title: The nonlinear utility guarantees rely on impossible approximation and representation claims
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-chaudhuri11a__I01 — The nonlinear utility guarantees rely on impossible approximation and representation claims
findings.markdown:
**Exact locations.** Section 5.1, PDF page 24 (printed 1092), the claimed Lebesgue formula and bounded-coefficient conclusion; Algorithm 3 and Lemma 23, PDF page 25 (1093); equations (21)–(22), PDF page 26 (1094); the utility derivation and Theorem 24, PDF page 27 (1095); Theorem 25, PDF page 28 (1096). Nonlinear-kernel generalization is promised in the abstract, PDF page 1, and is a separately listed main contribution on PDF page 3.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The paper asserts that its actual normalized random-feature procedure has the sample requirements in Lemma 23 and Theorems 24–25. Lemma 23 first compares with functions represented by uniformly bounded random-feature coefficients. Theorem 24 extends this to bounded-sup-norm kernel classifiers through a claimed implication from sup norm to bounded coefficients; Theorem 25 then applies that extension to a regularized population minimizer. $$

\omega\sim N(0,2),\quad \psi\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-\pi,\pi].

$$
|f_p^Tv(0)|\le\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt D},\qquad

\longrightarrow \log2-\log(1+e^{-1})>0.3798.

But equation (21) asserts that the **same** $f_p$ has excess risk

$$

For a fixed $\delta\in(0,1/4)$ this tends to zero along $n=D\to\infty$, for every fixed hidden constant. The two assertions cannot hold together, for any random-feature draw. The source of the contradiction is explicit. The cited Rahimi–Recht theorem uses **unnormalized** features and coefficients $|\alpha_j|\le C/D$. $$

findings.title: Logarithmic samples cannot control the stated full-distribution KL error
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-choi11b__I01 — Logarithmic samples cannot control the stated full-distribution KL error
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Definition 2, PDF page 9 / printed 1779, Equation (6); Theorem 11(ii), PDF page 23 / printed 1793; Appendix A.6, PDF pages 38–39 / printed 1808–1809, especially its last paragraph. Theorem 12 and Appendix A.7 inherit the claimed logarithmic sample order; the conclusion repeats it on PDF page 31 / printed 1801. The symmetric-discrete estimator and edge postprocessing are on PDF pages 21–23 / printed 1791–1793.

**Affected claim.** For a constant-effective-depth Gaussian or symmetric-discrete latent tree with $m$ observed variables, Theorem 11(ii) claims that $n>C'\log(m/\sqrt[3]{\eta})$ makes the probability of distribution-reconstruction error in (6) at most $\eta$. Equation (6) uses ordinary, unnormalized forward KL $D(p\|\widehat p)$, with any fixed accuracy $\epsilon>0$. The claimed constant must be independent of $m$ for the expressly stated logarithmic-in-$m$ guarantee. It may depend on fixed accuracy, failure probability and local model bounds. The proof transfers a structural guarantee to distribution error solely through one-to-one edge parameterization, overlooking error accumulated over a growing number of edges.

### An admissible bounded-degree, constant-depth family

Take observed binary variables $X_0,\ldots,X_r$ forming a path, with $X_0$ uniform and

$$
X_i=X_{i-1}\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}E_i,\qquad E_i\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/4).
$$

Attach a hidden binary node $h$ to $X_0$ and attach two further observed leaves $Y,Z$ to $h$. Give these three edges independent BSC crossover probability $1/4$ as well. Then:

- $m=r+3$, the only hidden node has degree 3, and maximum degree is 3.
- Effective hidden depth is exactly 1 under the paper's definition; observed internal path nodes are explicitly allowed.
- Every edge has information distance $\log 2$. The fixed bounds $l=1/4$, $u=1$ satisfy (11).
- The distribution has full support, a common binary alphabet, and no independent or perfectly dependent edge.

All edge parameters are fixed independently of $r$ and $n$.

Across $n$ independent samples, let $N_i$ count mismatches on path edge $i$. The transformation between path samples and $(X_0,E_1,\ldots,E_r)$ is bijective, so the $N_i$ are independent $\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/4)$ variables. Section 6.1's binary ML estimate is $\widehat\theta_i=N_i/n$.

On correct structural recovery, these observed–observed edge estimates are retained. Equations (24)–(25) recompute distances involving **new hidden nodes**, not these observed edges. The author implementation agrees: `RG.m` line 51 assigns the original observed-parent distance; `computeNewDistance.m` preserves distances between such parents; `contractWeakEdges.m` lines 9–20 skips edges with two observed endpoints. Eight native controls using the unmodified RG and CLRG functions retained every path edge with zero weight error. See native-check.m [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and native-controls.tsv [unpublished artifact reference omitted].

Marginalizing the hidden branch leaves the observed path. KL data processing and the tree factorization therefore give

$$
D(p\|\widehat p)\ge D(p_{X_{0:r}}\|\widehat p_{X_{0:r}})
=\sum_{i=1}^r \operatorname{KL}\!\left(\operatorname{Bern}(1/4)\middle\|\operatorname{Bern}(N_i/n)\right).
$$

The same obstruction thus applies even to the observed-marginal KL used in Figure 7, without any hidden-label or scale ambiguity.

### Self-contained finite probability certificate

For $N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/4)$, put $Z=(N-n/4)^2$. Exact moments are

$$
\mathbb EZ=\frac{3n}{16},\qquad
\mathbb EZ^2=3\left(\frac{3n}{16}\right)^2-\frac{3n}{128}
\le3(\mathbb EZ)^2.
$$

Paley–Zygmund yields $\Pr[Z\ge3n/32]\ge1/12$. On this event, Bernoulli Pinsker gives

$$
\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\operatorname{Bern}(1/4)\middle\|\operatorname{Bern}(N/n)\right)
\ge2(N/n-1/4)^2\ge\frac{3}{16n}.
$$

The events are independent over path edges. Chernoff's bound implies that at least $r/24$ edges satisfy them with probability at least $1-e^{-r/96}$. Consequently,

$$
\Pr\!\left[\sum_i\operatorname{KL}_i\ge\frac{r}{128n}\right]\ge1-e^{-r/96}.
$$

This does not rely on zero-count or infinite-KL endpoints. Hoeffding gives

$$
\Pr[\exists i:\widehat\theta_i\notin[1/8,3/8]]\le2r e^{-n/32}.
$$

On the complementary event all estimates are proper, and their distances are at least $-\log(3/4)>l$. The paper's contraction threshold and source lower clamps cannot remove the path-edge errors.

Fix, for example, $\eta=.1$ and any fixed KL accuracy $\epsilon>0$. Choose a fixed $C>64$ above both asserted sample constants (and the structural constant for failure probability $\eta/2$), and take

$$
n=\left\lceil C\log(m/\sqrt[3]{\eta})\right\rceil.
$$

Then $r/(128n)\to\infty$ while $2r e^{-n/32}\to0$. Intersecting the above event with correct structural recovery gives, for all sufficiently large $r$,

$$
\Pr[D(p\|\widehat p)>\epsilon]
\ge1-e^{-r/96}-2r e^{-n/32}-\eta/2\longrightarrow1-\eta/2,
$$

contradicting the claimed upper bound $\eta$. If the separate structural assertion failed instead, that would already defeat the theorem; it cannot rescue its distribution guarantee.

An optional estimator-independent check in risk-candidate.md [unpublished artifact reference omitted] uses edge probabilities $1/4\pm1/(16\sqrt n)$ in the same bounded-degree family. Independent binary testing gives probability above $.299$ of at least $r/8$ incorrect edge signs, hence KL at least $r/(1024n)$ on the correct structure. Thus pooling the particular homogeneous example does not restore a uniform logarithmic full-KL guarantee over the stated bounded-parameter class.

**Discovery method.** Traced Definition 2's unnormalized loss through Theorem 11 and the appendix's structural-to-parametric inference, then tested dimension accumulation on independent observed edge innovations. Checked the source for retention, contraction and any subsequent shrinkage.

**Verification method.** Re-derived the exact binomial fourth moment and finite Paley–Zygmund/Chernoff/Hoeffding certificate; verified constants with rational arithmetic and fresh binomial controls in risk-check.py [unpublished artifact reference omitted] / risk-results.json [unpublished artifact reference omitted]. Inspected the original rendered definitions/theorems and authentic author source. Ran unmodified author Matlab functions in Octave 10.3.0. Root separately read the relevant originals and reconstructed the probability argument in root-independent-check.py [unpublished artifact reference omitted] / root-independent-check.json [unpublished artifact reference omitted]; that was a bounded independent check, not a second full review.

**Confidence: high.** The counterfamily meets the printed assumptions with fixed local parameters, degree and depth. The contradiction has a finite probability proof, survives interior estimates and postprocessing, and was independently checked. Native output controls agree exactly with the estimator-retention step.

**Why this warrants rejection.** Favorable logarithmic sample complexity for distribution reconstruction is an explicit theoretical contribution, repeated in the main results and conclusion. Its error is not a constant or proof-notation slip: unnormalized errors from a growing number of parameters cannot be controlled with the advertised sample order. A dimension-dependent requirement, a per-edge/normalized divergence, or a materially restricted parameter family changes the central guarantee. The uniform lower bound rules out restoring it by a different ordinary parameter estimator on the same domain.

**Limits of the finding.** This does not refute fixed-$m$ consistency, the independent structural-recovery claim, the usefulness of RG/CLGrouping, or any particular historical stock/newsgroup ranking. The native implementation uses practical k-means grouping/general-binary determinant distances; the runs above are output-convention controls, not a claimed historical replication of the fixed-threshold theorem. Other source diagnostics and printed errors were screened separately and are not additional qualifying issues.

**The selected EP-FACT approximation can have no finite normalizing constant, even at an attracting EP fixed point for a proper smooth model.**

**Exact location.** PDF pages 3–5 introduce the factorized posterior-marginal construction; page 10, Equations (12)–(13), gives its exact starting identity; page 13, Section 4.2, selects the factorized approximation with alpha = 1; page 36, Appendix D, repeats the EP-FACT definition. The target model and scalar likelihood assumptions appear on pages 2–3. The affected contribution is the fast EP-FACT marginal construction, not the Jensen/Hölder bounds or the empirical claim that it can work well on particular datasets.

The paper starts from the exact identity

\[
p_i(x)=\frac{Z_q}{Z_p}q_i(x)\varepsilon_i(x)c_i(x),\qquad
c_i(x)=E_{q(X_{-i}\mid x)}\prod_{j\ne i}\varepsilon_j(X_j),\qquad
\varepsilon_j=t_j/\widetilde t_j.
\]

Its selected EP-FACT method replaces the joint conditional expectation by a product of conditional expectations and normalizes the univariate profile

\[
F_i(x)=q_i(x)\varepsilon_i(x)
 \prod_{j\ne i}E_{q(X_j\mid x)}\varepsilon_j(X_j).
\]

The following model meets the stated Gaussian-prior/scalar-likelihood setting, but \(\int F_1(x)\,dx=\infty\).

**Reproducible counterexample and assumptions.** Set

\[
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&3/5&3/5\\3/5&1&-1/5\\3/5&-1/5&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
Q=V^{-1}-\tfrac12 I
=\begin{pmatrix}19/2&-15/2&-15/2\\-15/2&37/6&35/6\\-15/2&35/6&37/6\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The leading principal minors of \(Q\) are \(19/2,7/3,1/2\), so the prior \(p_0=N(0,Q^{-1})\) is strictly proper. Let \(D=3+5\sqrt5\), \(a=3/D\), \(b=1-a\). For three observed Bernoulli successes, take

\[
t_j(x)=a+b e^{-x^2},\qquad j=1,2,3.
\]

Each likelihood is smooth, strictly positive and bounded by one. Thus the true posterior is proper and has all moments finite. It has a unique stationary point and maximum at zero: its negative log-density gradient is \((Q+\operatorname{diag}(2b e^{-x_j^2}/t_j(x_j)))x\), whose scalar product with nonzero \(x\) is positive.

Use the normalizable Gaussian sites

\[
\widetilde t_j(x)=s e^{-x^2/4},\qquad s=8\sqrt2/D.
\]

Their global approximation is exactly \(q=N(0,V)\). Every marginal cavity is \(N(0,2)\). Multiplying a cavity by its true likelihood and normalizing gives

\[
\frac38 N(0,2)+\frac58 N(0,2/5).
\]

This has mean zero and variance one. Its zeroth moment is \(a+b/\sqrt5=8/D\), equal to the site's cavity integral \(s/\sqrt2\). Therefore all three EP moment conditions hold exactly, including normalization; this is not an arbitrary Gaussian substituted for a converged EP output.

The fixed point is attracting for the parallel EP updates. The derivative of the new site precision with respect to cavity variance at variance two is \(-9/40\). The precision-update Jacobian is

\[
J=\begin{pmatrix}0&81/250&81/250\\81/250&0&9/250\\81/250&9/250&0\end{pmatrix},
\]

with spectral radius \(0.4765586113<1\). At the even fixed point, precision/linear cross derivatives vanish and the linear-site Jacobian is zero by the matched-moment response. Exact-form numerical iterations from neutral sites and the paper's suggested Laplace initialization also converge to this point; local attraction follows analytically from the Jacobian, rather than from those numerical traces.

For target variable one, both remaining conditional marginals have law \(N(3x/5,16/25)\). Since \(t_j\ge a\),

\[
E[\varepsilon_j(X_j)\mid X_1=x]
\ge \frac as\frac5{\sqrt{17}}e^{9x^2/68},\qquad j=2,3,
\]

and

\[
q_1(x)\varepsilon_1(x)
\ge \frac{a/s}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/4}.
\]

Consequently, for every real \(x\),

\[
\boxed{F_1(x)\ge \frac{675}{34816\sqrt\pi}e^{x^2/68}.}
\]

The normalization integral is infinite. Each individual conditional integral is finite; the failure occurs when their product is used to construct the marginal. Thus the page-13 phrase “always exists” need not be interpreted broadly to establish the error: the explicit selected marginal profile has no density on \(\mathbb R\).

The true posterior is independently expressible as an eight-component centered Gaussian mixture, by expanding \(\prod_j(a+b e^{-x_j^2})\). findings.title: The reported fixed-fraction precision exceeds the available positive examples
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-ertekin11a__I01 — The reported fixed-fraction precision exceeds the available positive examples
findings.markdown:
**Location and affected claim.** Section 4.1, PDF page 11 (printed 2915), defines Letter Recognition as A versus all other letters, with A positive. Section 6.1, PDF page 20 (printed 2924), specifies a 4,000-example test set and cutoffs for the top 50%, 25% and 10% of the list. Table 3, PDF page 21 (printed 2925), repeats this metric in its caption. Its Letter “50%” column reports mean precision from 55.61% through 90.96%.

Sections 6.1–6.3 use this table as controlled evidence that the new exponent improves top-list precision, that cost weighting improves it further, and that P-Classification outperforms AdaBoost and logistic-regression alternatives. The introduction, Section 5 and conclusion identify this analysis as a practical benefit of the equivalence relationship.

**Exact contradiction.** The [official UCI Letter Recognition archive](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/59/letter+recognition.zip) contains 20,000 rows and only 789 A examples. Independently downloading and counting it gives ZIP SHA256 `3b5f07a334697b6cace4fbae22940393a18fee596e73f68d97ce5973d52dc60f`.

The top half of a 4,000-example test list contains 2,000 entries. Even assigning every A in the entire source data to that prefix gives

\[
\operatorname{Precision@50\%}\leq\frac{789}{2000}=0.3945.
\]

Every one of the twelve Letter “50%” means in Table 3 exceeds this universal upper bound. The smallest is 0.5561; the largest is 0.9096. The bound holds for each split and therefore for their average, regardless of optimizer, convergence, seed or tie ordering. Standard deviations cannot resolve the contradiction.

If the intended 200 distinct A training examples are removed, the bound strengthens to $589/2000=0.2945$. The training sentence duplicates the word “positives”; its stated 1:5 ratio and later class counts identify the intended opposite class. The primary 0.3945 contradiction does not depend on correcting that sentence.

**Cutoff and protocol alternatives.** The displayed precision calculation in Equations (20)–(21), PDF page 19, uses $f\geq\gamma$. If $\gamma$ is a half-list percentile cutoff, that inclusive rule retrieves at least half the list and obeys the same counting bound. A strict rule that discards all examples tied at the cutoff could retrieve substantially fewer than 2,000 examples. Binary feature quantization makes that a relevant possibility. It is not ruled out as the behavior of an unknown implementation, but it changes the reported fixed-coverage interpretation and requires reporting the actual coverage and tie protocol.

An absolute score threshold, a cutoff within an already filtered positive sublist, relabeling the positive class, or oversampling tests could also produce larger values. None is disclosed as Table 3's protocol or authenticated by recovered code. These alternatives do not provide a result-preserving correction to the claimed controlled top-list comparison.

For example, the paper's own pointwise probability link gives

\[
f_p(x)=\frac{1}{p+1}\log\frac{\eta(x)}{1-\eta(x)}.
\]

All values of $p$ give the same ordering in this model. An absolute positive score cutoff instead applies an increasingly strict odds threshold as $p$ rises. Precision can increase simply by returning fewer examples, without improving ranking at a fixed list fraction. A replacement metric must therefore be disclosed and assessed with its coverage, rather than used to preserve the present ranking conclusion.

**Rejection consequence.** Table 3 is the principal held-out evidence for the paper's new precision-performance analysis. Its stated Letter results are impossible. The announced controlled comparison consequently lacks valid support and requires a corrected benchmark or a materially different, disclosed evaluation task. This is not a rounding correction or an identified caption edit known to preserve the claimed result. The exact minimizer-equivalence theory does not replace that missing empirical evidence.

**Discovery method.** A full-paper protocol and metric audit exposed the prevalence contradiction. The evaluation definition, positive-class orientation, test size, complete table and all claimed precision comparisons were traced before constructing the count certificate.

**Verification method.** All 25 original PDF pages were read. Critical protocol/table pages were rechecked in original renders. The author-hosted PDF is byte-identical to the journal original. The official UCI archive was independently retrieved, hashed and counted; the executable check verifies the exact rational bounds and the reported means. A separate parent reviewer read the relevant original pages, inspected critical renders and freshly downloaded/count-checked the official archive, confirming the certificate. That was targeted independent QA, not a second full-paper review.

```bash
python '[unpublished artifact reference omitted]
```

PDF 2, Section 1, calls the framework extremely general and says any generative language model can be the generator while an appropriate adaptor produces the power-law distribution. PDF 3 explicitly identifies the quantitative power-law fit as the second central contribution. PDF 6, Section 3.2, first defines the lexicon generator as a discrete distribution with independently generated lexical items, expressly allowing repeated word labels; its penultimate paragraph then asserts that an infinite-support generator transfers the integer adaptor's power law to frequencies in the final word sequence. PDF 10–11, Section 4.2/Equation (4) and Figure 4, give a valid PYCRP and exponent g=1+a, with a finite straight Zipf slope -1/a. PDF 15–16, Proposition 3/Section 5.3, give the equivalent stick-breaking construction. PDF 24, Section 7, and PDF 40, conclusion, again credit the adaptor with producing the word power law. Figure 4's simulated right panel is table occupancy, not word counts after aggregation over duplicate labels.

**Error and evidence: an exact model satisfying the stated assumptions.**

Use the paper's own PYCRP with a=1/2 and b=1. These are strictly interior valid parameters; the table-count power law has g=3/2. Use words w_j consisting of j copies of one letter, j=1,2,..., with fixed generator probabilities H(w_j)=2^{-j}. This is a proper discrete distribution with infinite support. A standard memoryless string generator emits at least one letter and independently stops with probability 1/2 after each letter. Lexical items are iid from H and independent of the adaptor, precisely as required in Section 3.2. No parameter or base distribution depends on the eventual sample size.

By the paper's Section 5.3 stick-breaking equivalence, let W_k denote the positive adaptor weights summing to 1; the iid generator labels L_k are independent of these weights. The actual word probabilities, after identical table labels are merged, are

\[G_j=\sum_{k\ge1}W_k\mathbf1\{L_k=w_j\}.\]

Every G_j is positive almost surely: infinitely many positive W_k and iid labels with H(w_j)>0 imply that each label appears. The word distribution therefore has genuinely infinite support.

Conditioning on the W_k and applying Tonelli gives the exact identity

\[E[G_j\mid(W_k)]=\sum_k W_k2^{-j}=2^{-j}.\]

Markov's inequality therefore gives

\[\Pr\{G_j>2^{-j/2}\}\le2^{-j/2}.\]

These probabilities are summable. The first Borel–Cantelli lemma, which needs no independence between the G_j's, implies G_j<=2^{-j/2} for all sufficiently large j, almost surely. Consequently there is an almost-surely finite random C such that G_j<=C 2^{-j/2} for every j. Sorting preserves a coordinatewise bound by a decreasing sequence, so the ranked word probabilities satisfy

\[\boxed{G_{(r)}\le C2^{-r/2}\quad\text{for all }r,\ \text{almost surely}.}\]

In particular r^s G_(r)->0 for every finite s>0. This excludes every nonzero finite-exponent power-law ranked tail, including the asserted PYCRP rank exponent 1/a=2. Equivalently, the number of words with mass at least x is O(log(1/x)), rather than the nonzero-discount power-law count of order x^{-a}. Conditional iid word sampling converges to these masses, so the obstruction concerns the model's actual long-run observed frequencies, not an unlucky small sample, finite-vocabulary truncation, or straight-line fit.

An entirely finite-sample companion check avoids stick-breaking and asymptotics. Let V_n be the number of different observed word types in n tokens. Each token has unconditional label probability 2^{-j} because the adaptor is independent of the generator. The union bound gives

\[E[V_n]\le\sum_{j\ge1}\min(1,n2^{-j})=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+n2^{-\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor}\le\log_2 n+2.\]

The infinite tail is summed exactly. This contrasts with the n^a table-growth process and does not conflate the two quantities. The mathematical contradiction is the almost-sure exponential bound; the finite-sample bound and simulations explain its source.

The event distinguishing lexical items from word types—independently generated items sharing a label—is ignored when transferring the table result.

Nor does it prove that the reported morphology accuracies or every particular generator have exponential tails. It invalidates the central generator-independent mathematical promise under the paper's own domain and the table-based justification offered for it. A nontrivial condition on the generator's label spectrum, with a new word-level analysis, is needed.

Enforcing a unique label per table (mentioned in PDF6 footnote1 as a more complicated optional generator) avoids this merging mechanism but changes the explicit iid discrete model, duplicate-word latent table interpretation and associated count damping used throughout the paper. Assuming that the generator already has an appropriate tail defeats the asserted independence from that generator and requires analysis of how aggregation changes exponents. **Exact location.** Theorem 3, PDF page 15 (journal page 1937); Gaussian model (2), PDF page 7; predictive construction and Equation (6), PDF pages 10–11; supporting Propositions 6–7 and proof of Theorem 3, Appendix B.2, PDF page 26. The abstract and Sections 5 and 7 advertise the affected pointwise consistency contribution.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** Theorem 3 says that a compactly supported, absolutely continuous true joint density and a full-support Gaussian DP-GLM base measure satisfying the unweighted finite-prior-mean condition give asymptotically unbiased pointwise regression estimates. These premises allow a continuous full-support base measure whose posterior prediction has mean **positive infinity at every finite sample size**, although the true regression mean is zero.

**Reproducible construction.** Use one covariate, alpha = 1, and parameters
theta = (mu, sigma, beta0, beta1, tau), with positive standard deviations:

\[
X\mid\theta\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),\qquad
Y\mid X=x,\theta\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x,\tau^2).
\]

Let \(p(t)=(15/16)(1-t^2)^2 1_{\{|t|\le1\}}\) and \(f_0(x,y)=p(x)p(y)\). This is a continuously differentiable, compactly supported probability density. Its true conditional mean is zero throughout \((-1,1)\); at the tested interior point zero, its covariate density is \(15/16>0\).

Let H have independent standard-normal mu, beta0 and beta1, and independent standard-normal log sigma and log tau. For every integer k >= 1, set \(s_k=2^{-2k}\), \(b_k=2^k\), and let \(G_k\) be uniform on the parameter box

\[
[-s_k/2,s_k/2]\times[s_k,2s_k]\times
[b_k,b_k+1]\times[-1,1]\times[1,2].
\]

Define

\[
G_0=\tfrac12H+\sum_{k=1}^\infty w_kG_k,\qquad
w_k=\tfrac72\,2^{-3k}.
\]

The weights sum to one. This G0 has a Lebesgue density and full support on the exact parameter space required by Theorem 1. Neither model (2) nor Theorem 3 imposes independence between the covariate and response parameter blocks.

The stated moment assumption holds even with an absolute value, for every real x:

\[
\int|\beta_0+\beta_1x|\,dG_0
\le \frac{17}{12}+\frac{|x|}{4}
+\frac12\sqrt{\frac2\pi}(1+|x|)<\infty.
\]

Indeed, the unweighted mean is \(17/12\). The construction even satisfies the stronger unweighted second-response-moment condition

\[
\iint y^2 f_y(y\mid x,\theta)\,dy\,dG_0(\theta)
=\frac{13}{2}+\frac23x^2+\frac{e^2}{2}<\infty.
\]

**Why the actual conditional prediction is infinite.** Every theta in the kth box satisfies

\[
\frac{e^{-1/8}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}s_k}
\le f_x(0\mid\theta)\le\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}s_k}.
\]

Consequently the base covariate density is strictly positive and finite:

\[
0<A_0=\int f_x(0\mid\theta)dG_0(\theta)
\le\frac4{\sqrt{2\pi}}.
\]

But each box contributes at least the same positive amount to its response-mean numerator:

\[
w_k\int\beta_0 f_x(0\mid\theta)dG_k(\theta)
\ge\frac{7e^{-1/8}}{4\sqrt{2\pi}}
\approx0.6161143.
\]

Summing gives positive infinity. The negative response moment is finite: on these boxes beta0 is positive and tau <= 2, while H has finite coefficient and scale moments. Thus the extended mean is well-defined as positive infinity.

This is not an improper-posterior example. For every finite sample D from the true support, the DP partition formula has a finite, strictly positive marginal likelihood. For a block of s >= 1 observations, its box contribution is bounded, up to a fixed factor, by the convergent series

\[
\sum_k2^{(2s-3)k}
\exp\{-s(2^k-2)^2/8\}.
\]

Adding the extra covariate density needed to evaluate the predictive denominator at zero changes the exponent to \(2s-1\), and this series also converges. H's corresponding integrals are finite because all its inverse-scale moments exist. The same bounds with a finite negative-response factor prove a finite posterior negative moment. These facts establish

\[
0<f_X(0\mid D)<\infty
\]

for every finite sample in the true support.

The exact predictive distribution on PDF page 10 always contains the new-component term

\[
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+n}
\int f_y(y\mid0,\theta)f_x(0\mid\theta)\,dG_0(\theta).
\]

Its positive response moment is infinite, and its coefficient is positive for every finite n. Therefore the exact joint-predictive conditional mean is positive infinity for every n and every such D. The specific latent-parameter conditional averaging formula in Equation (6) is also infinite, because each conditional retains this same new-component integral. This statement does not identify every possible posterior average of random-density conditionals with those two explicitly printed constructions.

The literal outer frequentist expectation in Theorem 3 cannot fix the contradiction: the predictor is infinite for every finite sample, whereas the true mean at zero is zero. The example uses the paper's explicit density-ratio predictor at an ordinary interior point; it does not choose an arbitrary null-set version of the true regression function.

Here those conditions permit an estimator that does not have a finite prediction at any sample size for a bounded target with a smooth regression function. Replacing the unweighted moment by an absolute moment, or even an unweighted second moment, does not repair it. A valid replacement must control covariate-density-weighted conditional tails and establish appropriate local convergence and uniform integrability. Appendix B's separate claim that weak consistency and absolute continuity imply pointwise density convergence does not supply that argument. This requires a different conditional analysis and a substantively narrower guarantee, beyond correcting a constant or index.

The counterexample does not establish failure of every stronger theorem, of the conventional independent product-prior examples, or of the paper's historical prediction-error rankings.

The executable certificate checks all rational moments, the density bounds and posterior-series ratios. Root independently read the critical original pages and reran an independently written symbolic certificate; this was a targeted second review, not a second full-paper audit.

findings.title: The central penalty comparison mistakes an overlarge sufficient tuning for inferior support-recovery performance
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-kolar11a__I01 — The central penalty comparison mistakes an overlarge sufficient tuning for inferior support-recovery performance
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF9–10 (journal2423–2424), Section3.3, Lemma5, Equation12, Theorem6 and the paragraph immediately following it. The inference is presented as a main contribution on PDF5/Section1.2, used in PDF10–14/Sections4.1–4.3 and Figures1–3, and repeated in PDF13–14/Section5. Model and penalty definitions are PDF3–4, Equations3–4.

**Claim.** The paper claims a sharp comparison of ordinary Lasso, the mixed(2,1) penalty and the mixed(infinity,1) penalty for exact union-support recovery. After comparing their sufficient conditions, Section3.3 concludes that the first two procedures have better dependence on task count k, and much better support-recovery performance once features are not perfectly shared. The simulations, which use Equation12 for the infinity-norm penalty, are offered as confirmation. The discussion suggests that this penalty might instead help for screening when false discoveries are less important.

The error is the inference about the penalty's performance. Theorem6 can remain a valid sufficient guarantee for its particular, overlarge Equation12 tuning. The calculations below do not claim it is false for that tuning.

**Error and evidence.** By the paper's own Lemma5, the mixed(infinity,1) estimator selects row i exactly when T_i=sum_j |Y_ij| exceeds its penalty lambda. For a null row, T_i has mean sigma*k*sqrt(2/pi) and fluctuations of order sigma*sqrt(k). Equation12 instead sets

lambda_paper = sigma*k*sqrt(2 log(k(p-s)/alpha_prime)).

It obtains this by bounding a sum by k times a maximum-coordinate tail. This is sufficient for controlling false selections, but cannot establish that the penalty requires its resulting signal strength. The entire excess above the null mean is of the wrong order.

Here is a valid calibration of the identical penalty under the identical model and false-selection budget:

lambda_cal = sigma*[k*m0 + Delta0],

where m0=sqrt(2/pi) and Delta0=sqrt(2k log((p-s)/alpha_prime)). The map z -> sum_j |z_j+a_j| is sqrt(k)-Lipschitz for any fixed a. Gaussian concentration therefore gives a null-row selection probability at most alpha_prime/(p-s), and a familywise false-selection probability at most alpha_prime.

For an active row let A be its number of activated mixture coordinates. Under Equation3, A is Bin(k,k^(-beta)). Define

c = sqrt(2 log(2s/delta_prime)/k^(1-beta)),

L = (1-c)*k^(1-beta),

Delta1 = sqrt(2k log(2s/delta_prime)),

d(t) = E|N(t,1)| - m0.

Chernoff's bound gives P(A<L)<=delta_prime/(2s). Conditional on A>=L and every pre-mixture signal magnitude at least sigma*t, the row's expected statistic is at least sigma*(k*m0+L*d(t)). Gaussian concentration gives the remaining miss probability at most delta_prime/(2s) whenever

L*d(t) >= Delta0+Delta1.                                      (A)

The union bound now gives exact-support recovery probability at least 1-alpha_prime-delta_prime. This controls the same familywise errors as the paper; it does not trade false discoveries for screening power. It is the same estimator (Equation4 and Lemma5), with a sharper valid penalty parameter.

A finite certificate uses a parameter configuration appearing in the paper's largest simulation: p=1024, k=floor(p*log2(p))=10240, s=floor(log2(p))=10, beta=1/4, alpha_prime=delta_prime=.01. Work in standardized noise units sigma=1 and put every pre-mixture nonzero coefficient equal to2. Multiplying all signals and penalties by the paper's sigma gives its noise scale without changing any probability. All observations are independent exactly as in Equation3; S may be any ten rows.

For these parameters,

- epsilon=0.09940884109588;
- lambda_paper=65983.88595945;
- lambda_cal=8656.20768458;
- L=893.54948860;
- d(2)=1.21909684443;
- L*d(2)=1089.32336190 > Delta0+Delta1=880.41570118.

Thus (A) proves that this infinity-norm estimator has exact-support recovery probability at least .98. The slack does not depend on delicate tail numerics: Jensen gives d(2)>=2-m0>1.2; the conservative bounds L>891 and Delta0+Delta1<881 already suffice.

For comparison, the paper's ordinary-Lasso tuning (Equation8) is lambda_Lasso=6.40860264271. Let Phi be the standard-normal CDF and define

pi0=2*Phi(-lambda_Lasso),

pi1=Phi(2-lambda_Lasso)+Phi(-2-lambda_Lasso),

pi=(1-epsilon)*pi0+epsilon*pi1.

Its active-row detection probability is exactly q=1-(1-pi)^k=0.005282696032. Independence gives exact full-support success

q^s*(1-pi0)^((p-s)*k) = 1.6900282592e-23.

Ordinary Gaussian Mills bounds already give q<.006 and hence full-support success below6.1e-23. The .98 versus1.69e-23 reversal is therefore an analytic counterexample to the claimed intrinsic comparison in a partially shared regime. It is not a Monte Carlo fluctuation or a request to try an arbitrary alternative hyperparameter.

This reversal also survives optimal calibration of ordinary Lasso within the paper's common-threshold family. Let N=(p-s)k. Null familywise error at most .01 requires 2*Phi(-lambda)<=1-(1-.01)^(1/N), hence lambda>=lambda_star=6.11461110732. Active-row detection decreases with lambda. At lambda_star its detection probability is only .01955486770, so every such false-positive-controlled Lasso has full-support success at most (.01955486770)^10<8.18e-18. The infinity-norm advantage is therefore not an artifact of keeping a suboptimal Equation8 threshold for its comparator.

The k-dependence also changes, not just a constant. Since d(0)=d'(0)=0 and d''(t)=2*phi(t), for0<=t<=1 we have d(t)>=phi(1)*t^2. In regimes with log(p/s) and log(s) of comparable logarithmic order, c bounded below1, and0<beta<1/2, condition(A) is met by

mu_min^2 = O(sigma^2*k^(beta-1/2)*sqrt(log p)),

provided this tends to0. For example take polynomial p in k and logarithmic s. This has the same polynomial task-count dependence as the mixed(2,1) guarantee and matches the dense minimax order in the paper's lower bound. The infinity-norm penalty can therefore be minimax-rate optimal in a partially shared regime, rather than having the inferior polynomial dependence inferred from Equation12. In contrast, the paper's Lasso needs a signal of logarithmic squared order in this regime. No claim is made that infinity-norm penalization is optimal in every sparse regime or universally superior to the mixed(2,1) penalty.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's main deliverable is the sharp comparison of the three penalties, rather than a new optimization algorithm. Its negative characterization of the infinity-norm penalty is inferred from a loose upper bound, and its supporting simulations use precisely the tuning responsible for that artificial loss of power. The counterexample preserves the model, estimator, partially shared feature regime and strict familywise error target, yet reverses the stated comparison with Lasso. A valid comparison must replace the infinity-norm signal analysis and rerun/reinterpret the comparative experiments; its dense-regime classification and the recommendation cannot be retained. This is a change to a central scientific conclusion, not a constant correction or an extra-experiment request. The lower bound and the substantive ordinary-Lasso-versus-mixed(2,1) results are not claimed refuted by this finding.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Lemma5 through Equation12, I compared the size of the proposed penalty with the null mean and fluctuations of the statistic it thresholds. The paper then inferred method performance from an achievable sufficient condition without a matching impossibility result for that penalty.

**Verification method.** Read all21 original pages, including every Section6 proof and the references; inspected original renders of the model, penalties, Lemma5/Equation12, comparative text, simulations and discussion. Re-derived the uniform false-positive/false-negative guarantee using conditional Gaussian concentration and the paper's Bernoulli activation model. Evaluated the finite certificate and exact Lasso probability with70-digit arithmetic, and checked conservative Jensen/Mills bounds. An independent reviewer inspected the original claim pages and reconstructed both the power certificate and the optimally calibrated Lasso bound with65-digit arithmetic; the results agreed. Source recovery found the author publication page and arXiv source but no authenticated historical simulation code; no historical numerical rerun is asserted.

Reproduction artifacts are calibration-check.py and calibration-certificate.json in [unpublished artifact reference omitted]. The high-precision computation is supplementary to the analytic inequalities above.

The analytic bounds have substantial slack, and the Lasso comparison has an exact product expression. The finding targets the explicit central inference about penalties; it does not misstate Theorem6 as an impossibility theorem or infer unpublished historical code behavior.

findings.title: Supervised feature fitting uses the probe-validation labels, invalidating the central population-quality evidence
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-montavon11a__I01 — Supervised feature fitting uses the probe-validation labels, invalidating the central population-quality evidence
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page11 (journal2573), §3.1, the training/analysis and two-fold-validation procedure; PDF pages5 and7 (2567,2569), §2.1, the distribution-quality and upper/lower approximation claims; Figures5–7 on PDF pages12–13 and their interpretation in §§4.1–4.2 on pages14–15. AppendixA on pages15–16 supplies the fixed-kernel statistical rationale being applied.

**Claim.** The method quantifies representation quality for the real learning distribution `p(x,y)`. After projecting onto the leading `d` kernel components, the two-fold test curve is presented as an upper approximation to the asymptotic real-distribution prediction error. The supervised experiments use these curves to support the principal hypothesis that progressively deeper representations become simpler and more accurate, and to interpret the preservation of statistical tractability.

**Error and evidence.** Section3.1 explicitly trains the deep network on all10,000 labeled analysis examples, stopping at2.5% training error. It then constructs the kernel representation from those same examples and splits only the subsequent linear probe into5,000/5,000 folds. Every probe-validation label was therefore already available to the supervised feature learner. Refitting the probe does not remove that label information from its inputs. This is a concrete path in the published procedure, rather than a conjecture about missing code.

The fixed-kernel argument does not justify this procedure. The cited Braun2008 paper, original PDF10 §3.3, explicitly relies on the eigenvectors depending on inputs only and being independent of label noise. A finite number of layers or widths does not control the label-dependent selection of the trained representation. Covariate-only kPCA on all points is not the identified error; supervised fitting of the representation on the validation targets is.

A reproducible counterexample shows the consequence even when `d` is much smaller than the sample size, the intended likelihood optimizer is used, and the network has exactly the study's2.5% training-error level:

1. Draw400 independent `X_i ~ Uniform[0,1]` and independent labels `Y_i` uniformly from `{-1,+1}`. For any predictor learned from this sample, a fresh label is independent of the prediction. Its population classification error is exactly`1/2`; its population squared error is at least`1`.
2. Set `Z_i=Y_i` except at10 selected indices, where `Z_i=-Y_i`. A continuous piecewise-linear ReLU feature map can interpolate `f_S(X_i)=Z_i`. Explicitly, sort the input knots `t_1<...<t_n`, let `m_j=(Z_{j+1}-Z_j)/(t_{j+1}-t_j)`, and use

       f_S(x)=Z_1+m_1(x-t_1)
              +sum_{j=2}^{n-1}(m_j-m_{j-1})max(x-t_j,0).

   Its sign classifier has exactly2.5% training error. The representation has consumed all labels before validation, as in the procedure under review.
3. For any finite positive Gaussian width, the mapped-sample kernel has entries`1` within each `Z` class and `rho=exp(-2/sigma^2)` between classes. It has rank2, and its leading two eigenvectors span the two class-indicator columns. A probe fitted on either fold consequently learns the two within-class target means/probabilities. Those features already identify the other fold's labels up to the2.5% deliberate corruption.
4. With NumPy seed`20261113`, alternating equal folds give probe classification error exactly`.025` and OLS squared error`.0978932852056705`, at each width`.1,.5,.9,1`. The binary logistic maximum-likelihood fit is finite: the four training-group positive-label probabilities are`1/50`, `49/50`, `1/27`, and`45/46`. It too has exactly`.025` validation error. Thus the result does not rely on an infinite separating logistic fit or the sign error in printed Equation2. The true fresh-data errors remain`.5` and at least`1`.

The exact rank/independence argument establishes the defect independently of floating-point calculation. With fixed-proportion label corruption, the probe error tends to`.025` and its squared error to`1-.95^2=.0975`; the population/probe gap does not vanish as sample size grows. This is systematic optimism, not the observation that an otherwise valid random estimate sometimes falls below its expectation.

An independent reviewer reproduced the construction using seed55181, obtaining finite logistic error`.025` and OLS error`.09867276266239174`. Perturbing its features by`1e-4 X_i` removes ties and makes all the paper's`.1/.5/.9` pair-distance quantile widths strictly positive. The corresponding two-component regression-probe errors are`.3703820`, `.0992232`, and`.0986729`, all below the exact fresh-error lower bound1. Hence the published width-selection rule does not repair the problem. Kernel centering likewise does not restore label independence.

These are counterexamples to the statistical validity of the analysis protocol, not purported reproductions of the particular MNIST/CIFAR architectures, their SGD paths, or historical numerical curves. The actual protocol defect is established by the original experimental description; the examples demonstrate why that defect prevents its claimed interpretation. No claim is made that the published networks memorized random labels or that their reported orderings reverse on an independent data set.

**Reason for rejection.** The central contribution includes a statistically motivated measure of representation quality on the learning distribution and its use to test Hypothesis1. All supervised evidence for that hypothesis uses the label-contaminated validation procedure. It can report highly accurate, low-dimensional task structure even when the distribution contains no predictive information at all. Its claimed population-error bounds and the resulting statistical-tractability conclusion are therefore unsupported.

The strongest narrower interpretation was checked: the conclusion calls the method descriptive statistics, and §4.1 limits observations to the experimental setup. Those phrases preserve meaningful descriptions of label-fitted training geometry. They do not withdraw the explicit real-distribution/upper-bound claims. Restricting the conclusions to training-sample geometry removes the principal population-quality interpretation and its validation; it is not a caption, constant, or normalization correction preserving the central result. Independent evaluation or a new valid statistical control of representation fitting is needed to support that main contribution. This warrants rejecting the paper as written, while recognizing the remaining descriptive insights.

This issue does not by itself invalidate the fixed-kernel idea, the transfer-task panels whose representation-training targets differ from the probe targets, or the separately trained full-data-set sanity-check accuracies. The latter do not validate the10K-network kernel curves.

**Discovery method.** Traced the claimed upper/lower error bounds back to the construction of their features and found that the two-fold split occurs after supervised feature fitting on the same labels.

**Verification method.** Read all19 pages, including AppendixA and references; rechecked the original rendered protocol, claims, figures and scope language; inspected the relevant original Braun2006/2008 arguments; derived the exact ReLU/two-centroid counterexample; ran the regression and finite-logistic controls and independent positive-quantile perturbation check. An independent original-page/severity review agreed with this narrow finding.

The author's later archived `kanalysis.py` was recovered and executed unchanged. It explicitly describes itself as similar to the analysis, contains a centered regression projection routine, and has no network trainer or validation driver. It corroborates low-dimensional projection behavior but cannot certify the historical2011 experiment. Original trained weights, exact10K selections, fold assignments and raw results were not recovered. The finding does not depend on a failed historical rerun.

Reproduction/evidence files are under `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`: `protocol-and-algebra-check.py` and `.json`, `gentile-independent-check.py`, `gentile-independent-controls.json`, `gentile-targeted-qa.md`, `cited-theory-check.md`, `native-check.py`, `native-controls.json`, and `kanalysis-recovery.json`.

**Confidence: High.** The validation-label path is explicit in the original PDF. The false population interpretation has an exact probabilistic and algebraic demonstration, finite-likelihood controls, an independent reproduction with the specified quantile rule, and an independent severity assessment. The report distinguishes that established flaw from unavailable historical measurements and unaffected descriptive/transfer results.

findings.title: Ensemble uncorrelatedness does not justify the single-realization intensity reduction
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2011__accepted__v12-omlor11a__I01 — Ensemble uncorrelatedness does not justify the single-realization intensity reduction
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 3.1, PDF12/journal1122, Eqs15–18; PDF13/journal1123, Eqs19–20 and the paragraph below Eq20; PDF14/journal1124, additional remarks1–2. The same error appears in Section3.2.2, PDF18/journal1128, Eqs31–32, and underlies Algorithm2/Section4, PDF21/journal1131, and the Fourier implementation/Section4.1, PDF22/journal1132. The claimed complete equivalence is in the introduction, PDF3/journal1113.

**Claim.** Under the anechoic model

\[
x_i(t)=\sum_j\alpha_{ij}s_j(t-\tau_{ij}),\qquad
E[s_j(t)s_k(t')^*]=0\quad(j\ne k),
\]

the paper first correctly obtains additivity of the **expected** Wigner–Ville spectra. It then replaces those spectra by deterministic Wigner transforms of a single realization in Eq18 and derives the positive intensity equations

\[
|\mathcal L(M)x_i(t)|^2
=\sum_j|\alpha_{ij}|^2
 |\mathcal L(M)s_j(t-A\tau_{ij})|^2.
\]

These are the equations solved in Algorithm2, Step1. Eq20 adds a residual and calls the equation approximate, but says it becomes exact asymptotically under the same zero cross-covariance condition. Remark1 explicitly attributes vanishing deterministic cross terms to uncorrelatedness without another approximation. Section4 concludes that uncorrelated sources suffice for the stated two-step solution. The paper permits mean-zero harmonizable processes with finite fourth moments, and Section2.3 explicitly chooses the unsmoothed deterministic WV estimator for its construction.

**Error and evidence.** Zero ensemble cross-covariance does not make the corresponding product vanish in an observed realization. The omission is central even for real, independent, smooth, finite-energy sources, positive nonsingular mixing and genuine unequal delays.

Let \(A_1,A_2\) be independent equiprobable signs and define

\[
s_1(t)=A_1e^{-\pi t^2},\qquad s_2(t)=A_2e^{-2\pi t^2}.
\]

Use

\[
(\alpha_{ij})=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
(\tau_{ij})=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/4\\1/3&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

These satisfy the stated source assumptions exactly:

- Each process has mean zero, and the two entire processes are independent. For every pair of times, \(E[s_1(t)s_2(t')]=E[A_1A_2]e^{-\pi t^2-2\pi t'^2}=0\).
- Their fourth moments are finite, their trajectories are smooth and square integrable, and their covariance kernels have integrable Gaussian Fourier representations \(\Phi_j(\lambda,\mu)=\widehat g_j(\lambda)\widehat g_j(\mu)^*\), where \(g_1=e^{-\pi t^2}\), \(g_2=e^{-2\pi t^2}\). Thus the harmonizability premise is satisfied.
- The two waveform shapes are linearly independent. The mixing matrix has determinant1. More strongly, the delayed Fourier transfer matrix has determinant \(2-e^{-2\pi i f(7/12)}\), whose modulus is at least1 for every real frequency. This example avoids a singular or instantaneous mixing degeneracy.

Take the paper's own Fourier choice \(\mathcal L(M)=\mathcal F\). At frequency zero, shifts contribute phase1 and

\[
\widehat s_1(0)=A_1,\quad\widehat s_2(0)=A_2/\sqrt2.
\]

The true source intensities inserted in Algorithm2 therefore predict mixture intensities \((3/2,3)\). The observed intensities are instead

\[
\begin{aligned}
|\widehat x_1(0)|^2&=3/2+\sqrt2 A_1A_2,\\
|\widehat x_2(0)|^2&=3+2\sqrt2 A_1A_2.
\end{aligned}
\]

For **all four possible realizations**, the residual is nonzero: \(\pm(\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)\). Its magnitude relative to the predicted intensity is \(2\sqrt2/3\), about94%, in each mixture. The residual is a continuous nonzero function on a frequency neighborhood, not a discrepancy confined to an isolated frequency. It persists when a longer record or finer sampling approximates these same finite-energy trajectories. In the time domain at zero the residuals are also explicitly nonzero: \(2A_1A_2e^{-\pi/8}\) and \(4A_1A_2e^{-\pi/9}\).

The correct identity retains the cross term

\[
|\widehat x_i(f)|^2
=\sum_j|\alpha_{ij}|^2|\widehat s_j(f)|^2
+2\operatorname{Re}\!\left[
\alpha_{i1}\alpha_{i2}^*
e^{-2\pi if(\tau_{i1}-\tau_{i2})}
\widehat s_1(f)\widehat s_2(f)^*\right].
\]

Its expectation is zero; the term itself need not be small. Accordingly, Eqs16–17 for expected WVS remain valid, while Eq18 and the deterministic intensity reduction do not follow.

The same distinction defeats the inference in Eq31: expected cross-WVS zero cannot imply realization-wise zero LCT products or orthogonal nonnegative intensity rows. For the sources above their unshifted time-intensity inner product is exactly \(\int g_1(t)^2g_2(t)^2dt=1/\sqrt6>0\), despite exact zero ensemble cross-covariance.

As a supplementary check, the problem also occurs for stationary ergodic sources. For independent iid standard Gaussian sequences, the unitary length-\(N\) DFT coefficients at zero frequency are independent exact standard Gaussians \(Z_1,Z_2\) for every \(N\). The omitted term \(2Z_1Z_2\) has the same nondegenerate distribution for every record length, with second moment4. Ergodicity or longer records alone do not make the unsmoothed power equation exact.

**Qualifications rechecked.** The paragraph after Eq20 acknowledges a residual, but its asserted asymptotic justification is the already satisfied ensemble condition. An unconstrained residual can absorb the cross term algebraically; that supplies neither equivalence nor a recovery justification for Algorithm2. Section2.3 discusses quasi-stationary smoothing as one possibility but does not impose a suitable consistency assumption or use such an estimator in the deterministic-power equations. The extra asymptotic intensity-orthogonality constraint on PDF18 may narrow the optional uniqueness claim there; it does not establish the earlier general reduction under Eq15. Adding pointwise disjointness, independent replicated observations and appropriate estimation, or a new recovery argument would substantially change the model or analysis. Simply inserting expectations requires different observables from the powers of the single signals supplied to the algorithm.

**Reason for rejection.** The principal contribution is the advertised theoretical framework reducing a general anechoic problem to nonnegative mixtures and phase retrieval, including its application to overdetermined mixtures without strong sparsity assumptions. The exact true source powers and true parameters in an admissible well-conditioned mixture fail the first subproblem of that reduction. Phase retrieval cannot validate this missing first-stage identity. Thus the paper's central equivalence and general algorithmic justification are invalid under its stated assumptions. Repair requires new substantive separation/observation assumptions or a new analysis, rather than a local correction that preserves the general contribution. The framework could still be used as a heuristic in favorable cases; that narrower claim does not establish the paper's central theoretical contribution. This finding does not assert that its reported empirical scores are fabricated or numerically reversed.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Algorithm2 back to its source assumptions, noticed that Eq18 substitutes an unbiased random estimator into an exact equation for its expectation and then drops cross terms. The intensity-orthogonality assertion in Eq31 provided a second indication of the same confusion.

**Verification method.** Read the full paper and AppendixA; rechecked original rendered definitions, equations, algorithm and qualifications. Enumerated all four sign outcomes symbolically, checked zero cross-covariance, Gaussian Fourier transforms, covariance spectral representations and the nonsingular delayed transfer matrix. Verified the time and Fourier residuals, seven sampling refinements and exact positive intensity inner product. Separately derived the invariant Gaussian-periodogram residual distribution. Executed unmodified later author-toolbox mixing and Fourier routines on16 cases with four signs/four sample sizes and unequal nonzero delays; native residuals match the exact prediction within1.47e-14. These later routines are a mechanism control only. Independent reviewer checked the original-page scope and exact counterexample. Reproducible scripts and results are in `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`, `exact-controls.json`, `native-controls.m` and `native-controls.json`; full-review notes and independent QA are retained there.

**Artifact limits.** The exact cited2011 ANMF download was unavailable after direct and archive retries. Recovered primary-site FADA material is from2014/2016 and is not evidence of the2011 implementation. Published figure data and historical runs were not reproduced. These limits are not used as evidence of an empirical flaw.

**Confidence: High.** The counterexample satisfies the explicit stochastic assumptions and avoids mixing degeneracy; each realization contradicts the central deterministic equation. The original PDF explicitly distinguishes expected and deterministic spectra, and the approximation/extra-constraint passages do not justify the stated general reduction. The finding is confined to that demonstrated theoretical failure.
